ops.title: Workflow Automation Essentials — n8n, Zapier and HTTP

ops.label: Should this be automated?
ops.detail: The lecture's closing framework. It opens with an intuition — do not automate what needs sympathy — and closes with the same idea made testable.

ops.label: Automate when it happens often enough that a human doing it by hand is the bottleneck
Do not when it is rare enough that setup cost outweighs time saved

A missing-item complaint on a food delivery app happens constantly — automate. A question asked by a handful of students on Discord is "an overkill — I can probably answer the question myself manually, which is what is expected"
Automate when the decision follows a clear, stable rule every time
Do not when it needs genuine judgement, empathy, or reading between the lines
A hospital call or a 911 call needs a human deciding fast on human understanding
Automate when stakes are low and easily reversible
Do not for binding prices, offers, or commitments

A reversible small exchange is fine. Air Canada's chatbot gave out a bereavement policy that did not exist — and the precedent set matters more than the payout: "if there is an AI bot making a mistake, the company is at fault"
Automate when errors are easy to notice and fix quickly
Do not when errors could run silently, unattended
"If error is not visible, you will potentially lose it and your AI will make a mistake"

ops.markdown:
> **What's the input trigger? What are the conditions? What's the output?**
>
> "Answer all three in one clear sentence and it's a strong candidate. If any honest answer is *'it depends'*, that's a job for a human."

**The mechanism is the sentence constraint.** You are not being asked whether a task *seems* automatable — you are being asked to produce a specific artefact, and **the artefact fails to form when the task is not.** "It depends" is the diagnostic, not a hedge.

The three slots are the canvas's own vocabulary, which is the point: the test is already the shape of the thing you would build.

The notes' thesis line, which this is the operational form of:

> **"The skill isn't clicking the right buttons — it's naming your trigger, condition and action before you open either tool."**

ops.title: What automation is for, and where it stops

ops.markdown:
Automation suits work that is **mundane and monotonous** — tasks that need attentiveness but no **"sympathy or emotional bandwidth"**.

> "You need to first be sure that what you're automating does require automation. And if it's a mundane task, does not require a lot of things, that is when the automation path can be taken."

**The test case, and why it is well chosen.** A guest complains that a hotel stay was bad. Capturing the feedback is mechanical. Being sympathetic, promising better next time, perhaps offering credits — that is human work.

The **same incident splits across the line.** It is not that complaints cannot be automated; it is that one half of handling one cannot.

**The awkward counter-case, raised in the same breath.** Support chatbots that **deliberately absorb frustration** — he named a retailer's returns flow that had irritated him personally that weekend. That is automation placed exactly where the rule says a human belongs, working as designed. Whether it is good design or a cost shifted onto the customer is the judgement the rule is asking you to make, not one it makes for you.

ops.label: Sheet entry
ops.detail: The entry point is interchangeable: "Whatever is your entry point — let's suppose there's a sheet or there's a WhatsApp entry… Insta, WhatsApp, any sheet, Gmail, whatever." The shape of the workflow does not change with the channel, which is why a Google Sheet can stand in for Instagram in the builds without losing anything.

ops.label: Condition
ops.detail: Bulk versus small is defined by **intent, not a field**. "I'm booking for myself and my family" is small; "I'm booking for the entirety of my colleagues, 15 or 20" is bulk. There is no number in the message to threshold on — which is exactly why an AI node ends up here rather than an IF.

ops.label: Irrelevant
ops.detail: "Is this even real?", "this looks surreal" — traffic that does not buy business.

ops.question: Three branches is the instructor's own class simplification — he agreed with a student that the real workflow would have more, since irrelevant hides a polite reply, a future prospect and a troll. What does this board do with that: leave the sketch as taught, or carry the fuller branching once Day 13 builds it for real?

ops.title: The diagnosis is speed, not quality

ops.markdown:
> **"It's not about the quality of your answer. It's primarily about the speed of your answer."**

**The lost booking.** A DM at **11:04 a.m.** asking specifically about the discount code. The customer booked with a competitor at **3:12 p.m.** Kabir saw the message at **9:47 p.m.** — eighteen hours late.

A *perfect* answer at 9:47 p.m. was worth nothing. Nothing about quality would have changed the outcome; **the entire failure is latency**, and latency is the kind of thing a machine fixes and a person does not.

The scale underneath it: roughly **4,700 Instagram messages** since a post went live, about **a third** answered, in whatever order the app happened to open. A separate WhatsApp inbox with its own backlog, cross-checked against nothing — so the same person can ask on both channels and get two different answers.

His comparison is food-delivery support, where an instant response is precisely why customers stay. Which is the same mechanism as the chatbot that irritated him in the opening section, seen from the other side: **absorbing the wait is the product.**

ops.title: The scenario run through the four criteria

cells.x-w: The lecture teaches the criteria in its closing section and the scenario in its second; it never runs one over the other. This row set is that exercise, done here.
Thousands of messages, about a third answered by hand. A person doing this by hand is visibly the bottleneck
The sorting rule is stable — bulk, small, irrelevant. Note it is stable without being mechanical: the decision is about intent, which is why the condition needs a model rather than a field comparison
A misrouted enquiry gets a reply in the wrong tone or a slow one. Nothing binding is committed, and it is recoverable

And the lost booking is exactly what an invisible failure looks like: nothing errored, nothing alerted, no queue showed red. The money simply went elsewhere and the only evidence was a message sitting unread. This is the criterion to design against when the workflow is built

cells.v-list: Node types — what you place on the canvas
cells.v-what: "What should be the agent that causes this workflow to start." The accelerator pedal — "the moment you put your feet on the accelerator, the car starts to move"
Text in, text out — used to turn messy human phrasing into a consistent value. "Just another node — text in, text out, nothing magic"
"If this happens then do this, else do that" — the fork
What starts the workflow: a new form entry, message, row, email, or a scheduled time
A check that decides which path the data takes next: a filter, an IF, a switch
What actually happens as a result: send, save, notify, create, update

cells.v-item: They are two lists, not one
cells.v-what: The class notes write the framework as Trigger / Node / Action on one page and Trigger / Condition / Action on another. Both are right: the first is the **node-type** list, where the AI/LLM node is simply called Node; the second is the **workflow-parts** mnemonic. They answer different questions

cells.v-list: Why the second list is the durable one
cells.v-item: "You'll forget which menu had which icon. You won't forget three words"
cells.v-what: Node types are a property of a particular tool's palette. Trigger, condition and action are a property of workflows, so they survive the tool changing — which is the point of teaching a vocabulary rather than an interface

ops.title: Where the AI node earns its place

ops.markdown:
Asked where AI fits, given that a five-o'clock trigger needs no intelligence at all:

**The trigger is usually mechanical. The condition is where language defeats rules.**

To route "bulk booking" with rules you would have to anticipate every phrasing — *I'm booking for 15 people*, *for my college friends*, *for my colleagues*.

> **"Will I be able to create all the possible rules in the world? No. That's why you need LLM."**

So the model's job is **normalisation**: convert unbounded human phrasing into **one of a small set of known values**, so that an ordinary IF can act on it.

That is narrower than "add AI to your workflow", and the narrowness is the point. **The model is not making the decision.** It collapses an infinite input space onto a finite one, and then a dumb comparison does the actual routing.

**Two extensions he added:** an LLM can also sit **in the action** — processing something that starts a further chain — and a workflow can run trigger → condition → action → condition → action indefinitely. The three words are a **grammar, not a template**.

---

**Board-derived, not the instructor's — the test that follows.** If the model's job is normalisation, then you are not testing whether it was *right*. You are testing whether it **returned one of your known values**. An answer outside the set is a failure you can detect mechanically; a wrong-but-valid answer is a routing error you will only find downstream. Worth separating, because the first can be caught by the workflow itself and the second cannot.

ops.label: Time is 5:00 PM
ops.detail: TRIGGER — and a scheduled time is the plainest kind there is. Deliberately mundane: the example carries no domain content, so nothing distracts from the grammar.

ops.label: Is the manager not looking?
ops.detail: CONDITION. "This becomes such an unseen leash — I can't leave early because the manager is looking, whereas I would want to leave early."

ops.label: Stay till 6:00 PM
ops.detail: ACTION — and this is the structural point. Both branches are actions. The condition selects between two outcomes rather than gating one against nothing, which is the same shape as the booking sketch, where ignore is a branch rather than an absence.
